content.text:
The gate names one failing sheet: FIG. 2, where the renderer attached the sensing connection to the wrong element and invented two extra dashed links. That is a drawing defect, so the repair is confined to the authoritative brief `figures/FIG-2.md` — no PNG is touched, and the claims, description and numeral table are unchanged because nothing in them was wrong.

Root cause: the brief gave the contactor and the connector current sensor identical shapes ("a small square outline"), and then routed the dashed sensing line "left below the horizontal run and clear of the control-pilot interface block" — a route that passes through the band occupied by the bus branch rising to the contactor and skirts the pilot block. That is exactly the ambiguity the render resolved wrongly.

Fix: give the connector current sensor a distinct circle outline, route the single dashed line straight up from that circle and out through the top of the channel rectangle where nothing else lies, and state explicitly that exactly one dashed line exists and that the contactor and pilot interface connect only through the isolated local bus. Numeral 124's leader entry is patched in the same answer to match the new shape.

Note on the record, per the drafting brief: no prior-art search was run for this application, so the art on file may be incomplete.

input.summary: Repaired the single failing gate item, the FIG. 2 semantic drawing review. The brief now gives the connector current sensor a distinct circle outline, defines exactly one dashed line in the drawing area, routes it straight up from the top of that circle and out through the top side of the channel rectangle where no other line work lies, and states that the contactor and the control-pilot interface are joined only through the isolated local bus. The numeral list entry for 124 is patched to match the new shape and to keep its leader clear of the dashed line. No PNG, SVG or other rendered artifact was edited; the drawing pipeline re-renders and re-inspects FIG. 2 from the amended brief. The claims, detailed description, drawing descriptions, numeral table and all other figure briefs are unchanged byte for byte, because the gate reported no defect in them and the invention is unaltered. Per the drafting brief: no prior-art search was run, so the art available for this application may be incomplete.

The shape-uniqueness statements (the only square outline, the only circle) were retained because they are what lets the numeral placement resolve 122 against 124 without adding invented geometry.

structured_output.summary: Resolved the single filing blocker from the previous QA report: the FIG. 2 brief was 3540 characters against the 2800 maximum and is now about 2700 characters of specification prose, with no geometry, part, or relationship lost. While trimming I found and fixed a genuine leader defect in the same file: numeral 124 (connector current sensor) was aimed at "the square outline straddling the horizontal run", but the brief identifies the square outline as the contactor 122 and the sensor as the only circle in the drawing area, so 122 and 124 would have landed on the same shape. Numeral 124 now targets the circle outline. I also stopped the FIG. 2 prose from naming the edge controller, which is not depicted on that sheet and whose numeral 106 is not listed on it; the single dashed line is now described by what it carries out of the connector channel, which is what the detailed description says the sensing connection does. No other figure file, no body section, and no entry in draft/numerals.md needed changing: FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 are within the length limit and their numeral lists match the table, so I left them alone rather than churn text that already passes. No review finding was left unaddressed and none appeared mistaken.
reasoning: The length overrun was concentrated in two places: a closing paragraph of purely negative linework instructions (no dashed line touches the contactor, no line joins the control-pilot interface to the circle, no direct contactor-to-interface line) and repeated restatements of connection points already fixed earlier in the brief. Negative bans on linework are exactly what a figure brief should not carry, so cutting them served both the character gate and the drafting rule. I replaced them with one positive sentence: every connection other than the single sensing line is solid. That preserves the discrimination the negatives were trying to buy, because the contactor and the control-pilot interface are already stated to be reached only through the isolated local bus branches.

I kept every disclosure-grounded element of the sheet: the dashed channel boundary, the vertical branch supply interrupted by the contactor, the horizontal run to the vehicle connector through the connector current sensor, the control-pilot interface block, the vehicle, the isolated local bus entering low on the left and branching to the interface and up to the contactor, and the one dashed sensing line. The shape-uniqueness statements (the only square outline, the only circle) were retained because they are what lets the numeral placement resolve 122 against 124 without adding invented geometry.

The 124 leader was corrected to the circle rather than correcting the prose to make the sensor a square. The detailed description gives the connector current sensor as an instrument measuring the current delivered through the vehicle connector and the contactor as the switching element in series with the branch; the brief's own body already carried the circle-for-sensor convention, so the numeral list was the side that was out of step.

Removing the phrase that named the edge controller in FIG. 2 avoids a part being named in a sheet whose numeral list does not carry it, which is the kind of mismatch the numeral check looks for. The edge controller remains fully depicted and numbered on FIG. 1 and FIG. 3, where it belongs, so nothing about the disclosed architecture changed.

I deliberately did not touch FIG. 3, whose prose names the isolated local bus and the branch current sensor as destinations of stub lines leaving the controller block. Those briefs passed the previous review, the stubs are edge-of-sheet connections rather than depicted bodies, and rewriting passing text would risk introducing new numeral or geometry defects for no gate benefit.

No claim, description, background, or numeral-table text was altered. The blocker was a drawing-brief length gate, and widening or narrowing the application text to answer a drawing check would invert the required order of authority, in which the inventor source governs the text and the text governs the brief.
